extracted.intended_audience: political leaders, public_relations practitioners, educators, and university administrators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on planning and executing propaganda/public-relations campaigns for political leaders, governments, women's organizations, educators, and colleges — covering staging, timing, messaging, organizational roles, and media relations. Emphasizes creating circumstances, dramatization, and institutional publicity management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create circumstances to dramatize the issue
rubrics_metrics.description: "create circumstances which would make his contention dramatic and self-evident."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use staged events and concrete demonstrations (exhibitions, exemplars, expert testimony, boycotts) so the public sees the issue as obvious before direct appeals are made; dramatization makes later speeches answer 'spontaneous questions' from a keyed audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate simultaneous exhibitions/events in multiple locations
rubrics_metrics.description: "stage a low-tariff exhibition simultaneously in twenty cities, with exhibits illustrating the additional cost due to the tariff in force."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Synchronize local events to create national drama and press interest; use consistent displays and messages across locations to magnify impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use prominent, disinterested inaugurators and endorsers
rubrics_metrics.description: Have exhibitions and events "ceremoniously inaugurated by prominent men and women who were interested in a low tariff apart from any interest in his personal political fortunes."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select endorsers who appear independent of the campaign to lend credibility; prominent inaugurators generate press coverage and convey legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mobilize affected interest groups to agitate and dramatize
rubrics_metrics.description: "have groups, whose interests were especially affected by the high cost of living, institute an agitation for lower schedules."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Activate constituencies with direct stakes in the issue to create authentic pressure and visible demonstrations (meetings, resolutions, telegrams).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use symbolic acts and behavioral demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.description: "dramatize the issue, perhaps by having prominent men boycott woolen clothes, and go to important functions in cotton suits..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ symbolic public acts (boycotts, dress codes, visible behavior changes) to dramatize the consequences of policies and keep the issue in public view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring expert/social testimony to humanize policy effects
rubrics_metrics.description: "get the opinion of social workers as to whether the high cost of wool endangers the health of the poor in winter."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use expert or practitioner testimony (social workers, physicians, teachers) to connect policy to real human consequences and increase moral urgency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prime the public before direct appeals (pre-exposure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attract public attention to the question before addressing them so that when the leader speaks he "would be answering the spontaneous questions and expressing the emotional demands of a public already keyed to a certain pitch of interest in the subject."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequence communications: first create awareness and emotional readiness with events and media, then deliver the core message so it resonates as an answer rather than an imposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time announcements to media cycles and news space
rubrics_metrics.description: Masaryk changed Czecho-Slovakia's proclamation date: "Czecho-Slovakia officially became a free state on Monday... because ... the press would have more space to devote to it on Monday morning."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose announcement dates/times to maximize press coverage and international cables; consider weekends, deadlines, and when newspapers have more space or attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid untrue or antisocial propaganda—truth/social purpose sustains effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: "The only propaganda which will ever tend to weaken itself as the world becomes more sophisticated and intelligent, is propaganda that is untrue or unsocial."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure claims are truthful and socially defensible; dishonest propaganda loses potency as audiences become more discerning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure substantive content — propaganda needs fertile ground
rubrics_metrics.description: "There has to be fertile ground for the leader and the idea to fall on. But the leader also has to have some vital seed to sow."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propaganda amplifies existing public concerns or legitimate ideas; it cannot manufacture resonance without some underlying substance or pre-existing receptivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda cannot substitute for real leadership or substance
rubrics_metrics.description: "propaganda is of no use to the politician unless he has something to say which the public, consciously or unconsciously, wants to hear."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communications should reflect authentic policy or values the public cares about; PR cannot indefinitely prop up empty positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use trial balloons and anonymous feelers to test reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: "trial balloon... send out an anonymous interview through the press. He then waits for reverberations... On the basis of these repercussions he then publicly adopts his original tentative policy, or rejects it, or modifies it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Float proposals or controlled leaks to gauge public and press response before committing; monitor meetings, editorials, telegrams, resolutions as indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plan propaganda with a clear objective and public knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: "The whole basis of successful propaganda is to have an objective and then to endeavor to arrive at it through an exact knowledge of the public and modifying circumstances to manipulate and sway that public."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define goals, research audiences, and deliberately shape circumstances (events, endorsements, timing) to achieve the objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train leaders in propaganda technique alongside civic education
rubrics_metrics.description: "the political leader of to-day should be a leader as finely versed in the technique of propaganda as in political economy and civics."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include media, messaging, and public-opinion techniques in leadership training so officials can lead public opinion rather than merely reflect it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create dedicated interpretative/public information offices in government
rubrics_metrics.description: "There should ... be an Assistant Secretary of State who is familiar with the problem of dispensing information to the press... The United States Government should create a Secretary of Public Relations as member of the President's Cabinet."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish senior public-relations positions with authority to advise and to advocate timely disclosure; staff them with people trained in media and public analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-relations official should interpret between government and public
rubrics_metrics.description: "He would, in short, interpret the people to the government and the government to the people... helpful in analyzing public thought and public trends."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The role combines analysis of public sentiment with clear presentation of government aims; serve as a two-way translator to keep policies intelligible and accountable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use propaganda as 'government by education'—create circumstances and high-spot events
rubrics_metrics.description: "Call it... government by education. But education... must be enlightened expert propaganda through the creation of circumstances, through the high-spotting of significant events, and the dramatization of important issues."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat public education as active PR: select and amplify events and discoveries that illuminate policy aims; dramatize complex issues into digestible public narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Map out legislative programs and use modern propaganda techniques to pass laws
rubrics_metrics.description: "They map out a legislative program and then use the modern technique of propaganda to make this legislative program actually pass into the law of the land."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocacy organizations should combine policy agendas with coordinated communications, grassroots mobilization, and publicity to influence legislators and public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use storefront exhibits and concrete demonstrations to recruit supporters
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumers' Committee example: rented an empty store and set up an exhibit tagging items with current and tariff-inflated prices; "Hundreds of visitors... rallied to the cause."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create tangible, sensory experiences (shops, displays) that let the public personally perceive policy impacts and be motivated to support the cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize clubs and women's groups to focus on specific community issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Women's clubs sponsor campaigns: cooking schools, milk in public schools, baby health stations, playgrounds, etc.; they "constitute an organized channel through which women can make themselves felt as a definite part of public opinion."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use organized groups to pursue concrete local reforms and public-education campaigns where they have special interests and competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educators must adopt a two-fold role: teacher and public propagandist
rubrics_metrics.description: "The normal school should provide for the training of the educator to make him realize that his is a two-fold job: education as a teacher and education as a propagandist."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train teachers to engage with the broader public, explain the value of education, and advocate for the profession — beyond classroom instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train educators in public outreach within normal-school curricula
rubrics_metrics.description: "the training of the educators... should begin in the normal schools, with the addition to their curricula of whatever is necessary to broaden their viewpoint."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include public-relations, communication, and community engagement skills in teacher training programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use public relations to raise the profession's status and secure better pay/conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Propaganda can "modify the general attitude toward the teaching profession" and lead to "an insistence on the idea of more adequate salaries for the profession."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame public narratives about teachers' societal value to generate support for improved material conditions and recruitment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universities must 'sell' themselves to secure public/state support while guarding academic integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: "The state university prospers according to the extent to which it can sell itself to the people of the state... yet if this is the case... its educational function may suffer."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance outreach and publicity to obtain funding without turning the institution into a mere political instrument; presidents must manage public image prudently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance donor/endowed interests with academic aims and use public opinion as counterbalance
rubrics_metrics.description: Endowed colleges may face donors with concrete objectives; "If the potential donor is apathetic, enthusiastic public approval must be obtained... If he seeks unduly to influence the educational policy... public opinion must support the college."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate public support to resist undue donor influence and articulate the institution's scholarly mission to potential benefactors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publicize scholarly research in accessible, dramatic forms via publicity staff
rubrics_metrics.description: "The popularization of this message... was due to the initiative of a young man named James W. D. Seymour... the oldest and most dignified seats of learning in America now hire press agents..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use press agents/publicity officers to translate technical findings into narratives that attract mass media and public interest; hire trained publicity staff with faculty approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create college news bureaus that uphold ethics and liaise with press
rubrics_metrics.description: Colleges maintain news bureaus; an intercollegiate association exists which "endeavors to uphold the ethical standards of the profession and aims to work in harmony with the press."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish news bureaus to regularize campus-media relations, educate alumni/public, highlight research, and coordinate messaging ethically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure publicity aligns with actual institutional quality — fix problems before promoting
rubrics_metrics.description: "If they [extension courses] have been badly planned... their effect may be the opposite of favorable. In such a case, it is not the work of the public relations counsel to urge that the courses be made better known, but to urge that they first be modified..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audit programs before promotion; public-relations should recommend substantive improvements when needed rather than merely amplify flawed offerings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct or emphasize institutional realities strategically (high-spotting)
rubrics_metrics.description: "If opinion that 80 per cent of the work is postgraduate research is false, it should be corrected by high-spotting undergraduate activities. If... true, the most should be made of that fact."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use selective publicity (high-spotting) to correct misperceptions or to amplify genuine strengths depending on institutional truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lend faculty to public investigations and advisory roles to increase relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: Cornell lent Professor Wilcox to census work; Professor Irving Fisher advised on currency matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage faculty participation in public service and advisory roles to demonstrate institutional value and generate attention for applied scholarship.
